Adult Sleek unicornfish (Naso hexacanthus) can attain a maximum recorded total length of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters], making it one of the larger members of the Acanthuridae family. This ultimate size is reflected in a substantial corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 12,105 grams [Wwi = approximately 12,105 grams], a mass that underscores the species' capacity for considerable somatic growth during its lifespan. Field surveys throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific region indicate that individuals reaching this size are likely among the oldest and most dominant within a population, often occupying prime foraging territories on reef slopes. Such large body dimensions are believed to confer advantages in both resource competition and predator avoidance, though the energetic costs of achieving and maintaining this mass are considerable. The extreme values observed in adults stand in stark contrast to the minute size of the species at its earliest life stages.

The onset of reproductive maturity occurs when individuals reach a total length of 45 centimeters [Lp = 45 centimeters], a benchmark that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 3,062 grams [Wwp = roughly 3,062 grams]. This size threshold is a critical demographic parameter, as it marks the transition to a reproductively active adult phase within the population. The mass achieved at this stage represents a substantial investment of somatic growth prior to the allocation of resources toward gamete production. Coral reef fishes often exhibit such size-related maturation schedules, and Naso hexacanthus appears to follow this pattern, delaying reproduction until a considerable body size is attained. This strategy likely reflects the high energetic demands of broadcast spawning and the need for individuals to compete effectively in the reproductive arena.

At the very beginning of the life cycle, the fertilised ova of the Sleek unicornfish drift as pelagic eggs before hatching. The yolk-sac larva that emerges is minute, with an initial wet weight at birth of only 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams]. This extremely low mass, typical of marine teleosts that produce numerous small propagules, reflects the pelagic spawning strategy and the reliance on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of development. After a period of yolk absorption, the prolarva must locate suitable planktonic prey to commence the exotrophic transition. Survival through this vulnerable phase is notoriously low, with the vast majority of individuals lost to starvation or predation before ever reaching the reef. The small size at birth imposes a significant bottleneck on recruitment success, as it is orders of magnitude smaller than the ultimate adult weight of over 12 kilograms [Wwi = over 12 kilograms].

Under stable thermal conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the species exhibits a maximum longevity of approximately 45 years [am = approximately 45 years], a lifespan that is notably extended for a reef fish of its body plan. Such a long life is characteristic of many large acanthurids and is thought to be linked to their relatively slow growth and late maturation. The sustained warm temperature appears to be conducive to physiological processes that minimize oxidative damage and cellular senescence, promoting extended survival. In warmer or more thermally variable environments, lifespan may be considerably curtailed. This remarkable longevity allows for multiple spawning seasons, contributing to the species' overall lifetime reproductive output despite a modest daily reproductive rate.

Field estimates of reproductive output under the same ambient temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] indicate that females release approximately 10,959 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 10,959 eggs per day], a daily rate that reflects the high fecundity typical of broadcast-spawning reef fishes. This substantial daily egg output is possible due to the large body size at reproductive maturity (roughly 3,062 grams) [Wwp = roughly 3,062 grams]. The constant spawning activity is energetically demanding, necessitating a constant intake of high-quality planktonic prey to sustain vitellogenesis. This strategy contrasts with those of many reef fishes that produce larger, less frequent batches of eggs, and it likely imposes a different set of selective pressures on adult foraging behavior and habitat use.
